title: Split a Number for the Biggest Product
statement:
You get an integer n. Write it as a sum of at least two positive integers and multiply those parts together.

Return the largest product you can get.

examples.why: The only split is 1 + 1. Keeping 2 whole is not allowed.
3 + 3 + 4 gives 36. Using three 3s leaves a 1, and 3 · 3 · 3 · 1 = 27 is worse.

hints: Call best[k] the biggest product for k. If the first part is j, the rest k − j can either stay whole or be split further.
So best[k] = max over j of j · max(k − j, best[k − j]). The max is there because splitting is optional for the remainder, but not for n itself.
Look at the answers: they are made of 3s, with a 2 or two thrown in. Any part of 5 or more can be split into a bigger product, and 3 + 1 should become 2 + 2.

explain.intuition:
Choose the first part j. What is left, k − j, is either kept as one part or split again, and the best split of it is a smaller version of the same problem. That gives a DP over k = 2..n. The only twist: for the remainder, "don't split" is allowed, so compare k − j with best[k − j]. For n itself at least one cut is required, which the outer loop over j forces.

The DP also reveals a pattern. A part p ≥ 5 is never optimal because 3 · (p − 3) > p. A 4 can be 2 + 2 at no loss. A 1 wastes a unit. So the best split uses as many 3s as possible, and if a remainder of 1 would appear, one 3 + 1 turns into 2 + 2.
steps: For each k from 2 to n, try every first part j from 1 to k − 1.
Candidate: j · max(k − j, best[k − j]). Keep the largest as best[k].
Return best[n]. (Closed form: for n ≤ 3 return n − 1; otherwise take 3s while more than 4 is left, then multiply by the rest.)
pitfalls: Letting n stay whole. For n = 2 or 3 the answer is n − 1, not n.
Using best[k − j] without comparing to k − j. For small remainders like 2 or 3, leaving them whole is better than splitting them.
Greedily taking 3s all the way down. When 1 is left over, you need 2 + 2 instead of 3 + 1.

complexity.time: O(n²) for the DP, O(n) for the 3s rule
complexity.space: O(n) for the DP, O(1) for the 3s rule

solutions.title: DP over the first part
solutions.idea: best[k] = max over j of j · max(k − j, best[k − j]). Each remainder may be kept or split further.

solutions.title: As many 3s as possible
solutions.idea: Parts of 5 or more can always be split for a bigger product, and 3 + 1 is worse than 2 + 2. So take 3s while more than 4 remains.

followups: Prove that a part of 5 or more is never in an optimal split.
If n can be up to 10⁹ and you return the product modulo 10⁹ + 7, how do you compute it quickly?
